newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - Exabyte fights back with new products.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Exabyte fights back with new products.

text.p: After two years of choppy performance, tape storage company Exabyte Corp is fighting to return to growth with new higher-capacity and faster-speed products, chairman Peter Behrendt said on Monday.

"The last two years have been transition years for Exabyte. We are taking the company through a number of significant changes which we expect to start paying off in 1997 and beyond," Behrendt told Reuters in an interview.
He said Exabyte expected to return to profit in the first quarter this year after reporting a net loss of US$2.04 million in the last quarter of 1996 on revenue of US$85.9 million.

Overall, 1996 was profitable with a net income of US$8.6 million after 1995's net loss of US$12.4 million. Inventory write-downs, reserves and goodwill write-offs dragged Exabyte into the red in 1995 despite higher revenues of US$374.1 million compared to 1996's US$362.9 million.
Behrendt said the company's performance was hindered by relatively old 8mm tape drives, which were its core products.

"We have essentially been shipping three-year old products for 1996, and in 1997 we are introducing and shipping replacement products which we think are among the most competitive in the industry," he said.
"We are going to convince people we have the products to resume growth," Behrendt said.
First off the mark in 1997 was a new flagship 8mm high capacity, high-speed tape drive named Mammoth.

It offers 40 Gigabyte of capacity and is able to read and write data at a rate of 6 megabytes per second -- six times the speed and almost three times the capacity of its older generation 8505XL 8mm tape drive, he said.

Mammoth is part of the company's high performance Entura line targetted at the high-end work station and networks market. Another new 8mm tape drive, the Eliant 820, is twice as fast as its predecessor but offered at a lower price. The Eliant line is focused on the Windows NT market.
Behrendt said the 8mm tape drive products contributed 60-65 percent of the company's revenue.
Exabyte was looking to introduce tape drives with capacity of 150 GB with speed of up to 18.85 MB per second by the end of the decade, he said.
The new 8mm products are expected to generate benefits for its library business as well. In a library, robotics control the a system of tapes and tape drives.
Exabyte was moving into the smaller systems market like personal computers with a concept called "Nest", part of its lower-priced tape drives Eagle division, Behrendt said.
A "nest" is a low-cost receptable installed into a slot in PC. The user can share a tape drive among a number of PCs by sliding it into the "nest", without any cabling or wiring.
The "nest" allows other types of storage devices to be used like zip drives or another hard disk drive.
The Eagle division contributed five percent to Exabyte's revenue in 1996 and Behrendt saw tremendous growth with the cost-reducing nest concept.
He said Exabyte achieved average gross margins of 25-30 percent in 1996 and was aiming to maintain them.
Revenue from outside the United States now made up 30-35 percent of the company's total sales and this could move to 50 percent in the next five years, Behrendt said.
